props.title: Chances Are

sections.content: Chances Are (1989) stands as a charming reincarnation romance that puts a clever spin on the supernatural love story genre. Robert Downey Jr. shines as a young man who gradually realizes he's the reincarnation of Cybill Shepherd's dead husband, creating an unusual love triangle with both Shepherd and her daughter (Mary Stuart Masterson). The film follows in the footsteps of Heaven Can Wait (1978) and All of Me (1984) in its playful handling of soul-switching, but adds a uniquely complex emotional layer by exploring the ethics of past-life romance.

sections.content: The late 1980s and early 1990s saw a surge of supernatural romance films that mixed comedy with metaphysical themes. Ghost (1990) became the genre's biggest hit, while films like Always (1989) and Made in Heaven (1987) explored similar territory of love transcending death. What sets Chances Are apart is its willingness to wrestle with ethical dilemmas - should a reincarnated soul pursue their former spouse? The film manages to be both funny and thought-provoking while avoiding the darker elements of similar films.

Director Emile Ardolino, fresh off Dirty Dancing (1987), brings a light touch to material that could have become either too heavy or too silly. The chemistry between Downey Jr. and Shepherd feels genuine, while Ryan O'Neal provides solid support as the friend who's quietly loved Shepherd's character for years. The film's exploration of memory and identity predates later metaphysical romances like The Lake House (2006) and The Time Traveler's Wife (2009). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: While not as commercially successful as Ghost, Chances Are helped establish a template for supernatural romances that balanced comedy, drama, and metaphysical elements. Its influence can be seen in later films like Just Like Heaven (2005) and P.S. I Love You (2007), which similarly deal with love that transcends death but maintains a lighter tone. The film also represents an important early dramatic role for Robert Downey Jr., showcasing his ability to handle both comedy and emotional depth.
